summary: Defines the wire image, an abstraction of the information a protocol exposes to an on-path observer that is not a participant. The idea helps explain what happens to network functions that rely on seeing traffic when more of it is encrypted. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Imagine mail carriers who can read only what is written on the outside of an envelope. The wire image is everything they can see, and this document is about what happens when less of it is visible.

questions: how does encryption affect network functions
subtitle: A name for everything a protocol shows to observers on the path, and why it matters as encryption spreads.

tldr.problem: More encryption hides protocol information from devices on the network path, but there was no shared way to talk about what those devices can still see and use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the wire image: the packets seen by an observer who is not part of the communication, including their content, timing and the observer's vantage point.
tldr.outcome: Protocol designers can engineer the wire image on purpose, exposing only what is needed and declaring invariants, so that visible bits do not become frozen by devices on the path.

today: RFC 8546 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the IAB's definition of the wire image as an abstraction for discussing encryption and network functions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A protocol specification defines the behavior of each participant. Implicit in it is the information the protocol radiates toward nonparticipant observers. Any information that is clearly defined by the message format, or implied by it, and is not cryptographically confidentiality protected, can be interpreted unambiguously by those observers. That information is the protocol's wire image.

The RFC argues that the wire image, not the specification, determines how third parties on the path interact with a protocol. Deployment of transport-layer security (RFC 8446) and transports with encrypted control information such as QUIC make this newly relevant. QUIC is described as the first IETF-defined transport protocol to minimize its own wire image to prevent ossification and improve end-to-end privacy. The document treats the wire image as a pure abstraction to shed light on the ongoing debate.
sections.eli5: Everything you do in public can be seen by people walking by. This document gives a name to what a network can see of your messages.

sections.title: Definition and Properties
sections.content:
The wire image of the protocols in use is their view as observed by an entity not participating in the communication. It is the sequence of packets sent by each participant, including their content and metadata about the observation: the time each packet is seen and the observer's vantage point.

The wire image is therefore not just the unencrypted header bits. Interpacket timing and packet sizes can reveal other protocol behavior or fingerprint protocols and implementations. Each observer may see a slightly different image, since the image depends on where it is taken.

Portions that are neither confidentiality nor integrity protected are writable by devices on the path, and a device that understands them can modify them to induce behavior in the participants. TCP is given as an example. The wire image can be taken for a single packet, a single protocol, or the whole stack. In practice a passive observer combines all packets of a conversation, correlates protocols such as DNS with the application, and adds other context. The RFC notes that the image is multidimensional, so image recognition techniques may be applicable.
sections.eli5: It is not only the words on the envelope. How big it is and when it arrives tell a story too, and each carrier sees it from where they stand.

sections.title: Hiding, Protecting and Engineering
sections.content:
Cryptography can hide headers that forwarding devices do not need. Techniques against timing analysis can reduce metadata, but have limits: packets cannot be smaller than their information content or faster than the speed of light, and the techniques cost bandwidth and latency.

End-to-end integrity protection makes parts of the wire image effectively immutable, since on-path devices cannot change them without the endpoints detecting it, although they can still read them. That lets endpoints create signals meant only for on-path devices. Interarrival timings and message sequences cannot be protected this way, because delays, drops and reordering are normal in the network.

The RFC's general principle is that all observable parts of a protocol's wire image will eventually be used by devices on path, so changes to them become difficult or impossible to deploy. For example, TCP's headers are inseparable from its operation and are used by firewalls for return routability and consent, and for measuring loss and latency. Designers should expose deliberately the information they want the network to use and as little else as possible.
sections.eli5: If you leave a note where everyone can read it, people will start to depend on it, and you can never change it. So share only what you mean to share.

sections.title: Invariants and Trust in Signals
sections.content:
One approach is to declare protocol invariants, a promise that certain bits and observable behaviors will be preserved in all future versions. QUIC's invariants are an initial attempt. Bits with simple semantics at fixed positions, and those implementing version negotiation, suit invariants. More fluid behavior does not.

Parts that are visible but not invariant should be protected against accidental invariance, where devices make simplifying assumptions that make new behavior hard to deploy. Integrity protection can help, and so can the techniques in the cited use-it-or-lose-it draft. Parts not meant to be visible should be encrypted.

Signals engineered to be exposed are separate from the encrypted protocol's own mechanisms, so on-path devices may be unable to verify them (see RFC 8558). Two endpoints with a secret channel may collude to change what these signals mean.
sections.eli5: Promise that some parts will never change, lock away the rest, and remember that a sign you put up for others might not always be telling the truth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document explores information exposed by the wire image that may matter for end-to-end privacy and security. Designers must take care to expose only what the design deems necessary, and must work to reduce the risk that information not explicitly included can be derived from observation. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Only show what you must, and watch out for clues that give away more than you meant.

items.title: Packets
items.text: The sequence of packets sent by each participant.

items.title: Content
items.text: What those packets contain, as far as it is not confidentiality protected.

items.title: Timing
items.text: The time at which each packet is observed.

items.title: Vantage point
items.text: Where the observer sits, so each observer may see a different image.
